subtitle: Questions 1–20 · detailed solutions

sections.title: Single Correct Type
marking: Marking not printed in the paper; JEE Advanced default assumed:

concepts: Projection of a vector on another vector
questions.question: If $\vec a$ is a nonzero vector such that its projections on the vectors $2\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k$, $\hat i+2\hat j-2\hat k$ and $\hat k$ are equal, then a unit vector along $\vec a$ is:
questions.key_idea: Equal projections on three vectors give two linear equations in the components of $\vec a$, enough to fix its direction.
solution: Let $\vec a=a_1\hat i+a_2\hat j+a_3\hat k$ with $a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2=1$ (unit vector).
Let $\vec b=2\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k$, $\vec c=\hat i+2\hat j-2\hat k$, $\vec d=\hat k$; note $|\vec b|=|\vec c|=3$ and $|\vec d|=1$.
Equal projections: $\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec b|}=\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec c}{|\vec c|}=\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|}$.
First equality with the third: $2a_1-a_2+2a_3=3a_3$, so $a_3=2a_1-a_2$. Second with the third: $a_1+2a_2-2a_3=3a_3$, so $a_1+2a_2=5a_3$.
So the unit vector is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{155}}\left(7\hat i+9\hat j+5\hat k\right)$, which is option (2).

alternate_solutions.idea: Equal projections mean $\vec a$ is perpendicular to the differences of the unit vectors, so $\vec a$ is along their cross product.
solution: Projection of $\vec a$ on $\vec v$ is $\vec a\cdot\hat v$. Equal projections on $\hat b,\hat c,\hat k$ mean $\vec a\cdot(\hat b-\hat k)=0$ and $\vec a\cdot(\hat c-\hat k)=0$.
$\hat b=\frac13(2,-1,2)$ and $\hat c=\frac13(1,2,-2)$, so $\hat b-\hat k=\frac13(2,-1,-1)$ and $\hat c-\hat k=\frac13(1,2,-5)$.
$\vec a$ is perpendicular to both, so it is parallel to their cross product: $(2,-1,-1)\times(1,2,-5)=\left((-1)(-5)-(-1)(2),\ (-1)(1)-2(-5),\ 2\cdot2-(-1)(1)\right)=(7,9,5)$.

The sign: for $-(7,9,5)$ all three projections would be negative but still equal, so both signs satisfy the condition; only $+\frac{1}{\sqrt{155}}(7,9,5)$ appears among the options, which is option (2).

useful_results: The projection of $\vec a$ on $\vec v$ is the scalar $\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec v}{|\vec v|}=\vec a\cdot\hat v$ (signed); the vector projection is $(\vec a\cdot\hat v)\hat v$.

Equal projections on $\vec v_1,\vec v_2$ means $\vec a\perp(\hat v_1-\hat v_2)$: $\vec a$ lies in a plane through the origin, and two such conditions fix $\vec a$ up to a scalar (a line), $\vec a\parallel(\hat v_1-\hat v_2)\times(\hat v_1-\hat v_3)$.
A direction fixed by two orthogonality conditions is always the cross product of the two normals; the length then comes from the normalisation, with a $\pm$ sign unless the question fixes it.

concepts: Vector (cross) product and scalar triple product identities
questions.question: Let $\vec a=2\hat i-3\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec b=3\hat i+2\hat j+5\hat k$ and a vector $\vec c$ be such that $(\vec a-\vec c)\times\vec b=-18\hat i-3\hat j+12\hat k$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec c=3$. If $\vec b\times\vec c=\vec d$, then $|\vec a\cdot\vec d|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Expanding $(\vec a-\vec c)\times\vec b$ produces $\vec b\times\vec c=\vec d$, and dotting with $\vec a$ kills $\vec a\times\vec b$.
solution: Given $(\vec a-\vec c)\times\vec b=-18\hat i-3\hat j+12\hat k$.
Expand: $\vec a\times\vec b-\vec c\times\vec b=-18\hat i-3\hat j+12\hat k$.
Since $-\vec c\times\vec b=\vec b\times\vec c=\vec d$, this reads $\vec a\times\vec b+\vec d=-18\hat i-3\hat j+12\hat k$.
Take the dot product with $\vec a$. Because $\vec a\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=0$, we get $\vec a\cdot\vec d=\vec a\cdot\left(-18\hat i-3\hat j+12\hat k\right)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $\vec d$ itself: $\vec d=\vec w-\vec a\times\vec b$, then dot with $\vec a$ and check $\vec d\perp\vec b$.
solution: Let $\vec w=-18\hat i-3\hat j+12\hat k$. From $\vec a\times\vec b+\vec d=\vec w$ we have $\vec d=\vec w-\vec a\times\vec b$.
Check: $\vec d=\vec b\times\vec c$ must be perpendicular to $\vec b$: $\vec b\cdot\vec d=-3+8-5=0$, consistent.
The condition $\vec a\cdot\vec c=3$ is not needed for this value; it only makes the choice of $\vec c$ unique.

useful_results: $\vec a\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=0$ and $\vec b\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=0$: dotting a vector equation with one of the vectors in a cross product removes that term.
$\vec x\times\vec b=\vec w$ is solvable only if $\vec w\perp\vec b$ (here $\vec b\cdot\vec w=-54-6+60=0$), and then $\vec x$ is determined up to adding a multiple of $\vec b$.
Cross product is anti-commutative and distributive: $(\vec a-\vec c)\times\vec b=\vec a\times\vec b+\vec b\times\vec c$. Quickly spotting this converts the given into the definition of $\vec d$.
Extra data in vector questions (like $\vec a\cdot\vec c=3$ here) is often only a consistency or uniqueness condition; do not force it into the main computation.

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines
questions.question: The line $L_1$ is parallel to the vector $\vec a=-3\hat i+2\hat j+4\hat k$ and passes through the point $(7,6,2)$, and the line $L_2$ is parallel to the vector $\vec b=2\hat i+\hat j+3\hat k$ and passes through the point $(5,3,4)$. The shortest distance between the lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ is:
questions.key_idea: Shortest distance is the component of the join of the two points along $\vec b_1\times\vec b_2$.
solution: $L_1:\ \vec r=7\hat i+6\hat j+2\hat k+\lambda\left(-3\hat i+2\hat j+4\hat k\right)$.
$L_2:\ \vec r=5\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k+\mu\left(2\hat i+\hat j+3\hat k\right)$.
Shortest distance $=\left|\frac{(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}\right|$ with $\vec a_2-\vec a_1=-2\hat i-3\hat j+2\hat k$.
Numerator: $(-2\hat i-3\hat j+2\hat k)\cdot(2\hat i+17\hat j-7\hat k)=-4-51-14=-69$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Minimise the distance between a point of each line: the common perpendicular makes the join perpendicular to both directions.
solution: Solving the two linear equations gives $\lambda=\frac{20}{57}$ and $\mu=\frac{31}{114}$.
Substituting back gives $|\overrightarrow{PQ}|=\frac{23}{\sqrt{38}}$ (checked by direct evaluation), the same answer.

useful_results: Shortest distance between skew lines $\vec r=\vec a_1+\lambda\vec b_1$ and $\vec r=\vec a_2+\mu\vec b_2$ is $\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)|}{|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|}$; it is $0$ exactly when the lines intersect (or are coplanar and non-parallel).
For parallel lines use $\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\times\vec b|}{|\vec b|}$ instead; the cross-product denominator would be zero.
Cross-product magnitude without computing the cross product: $|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2|^2=|\vec b_1|^2|\vec b_2|^2-(\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2)^2$. Here $29\cdot14-8^2=342$, matching $\sqrt{342}$.
Cleaning the answer: $\frac{69}{\sqrt{342}}$ simplifies using $342=9\cdot38$.

concepts: Angle between vectors and resolution into parallel and perpendicular components
questions.question: Consider two vectors $\vec u=3\hat i-\hat j$ and $\vec v=2\hat i+\hat j-\lambda\hat k$, $\lambda>0$. The angle between them is given by $\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt5}{2\sqrt7}\right)$. Let $\vec v=\vec v_1+\vec v_2$, where $\vec v_1$ is parallel to $\vec u$ and $\vec v_2$ is perpendicular to $\vec u$. Then the value of $|\vec v_1|^2+|\vec v_2|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Since $\vec v_1\perp\vec v_2$, $|\vec v_1|^2+|\vec v_2|^2=|\vec v|^2$ once $\lambda$ is known.
solution: $\lambda^2=9$, so $\lambda=3$ (as $\lambda>0$), and $\vec v=2\hat i+\hat j-3\hat k$.
Write $\vec v_1=\alpha\vec u=\alpha(3\hat i-\hat j)$. Then $\vec v_2=\vec v-\vec v_1=(2-3\alpha)\hat i+(1+\alpha)\hat j-3\hat k$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Pythagoras: $\vec v_1\perp\vec v_2$, so the required sum is just $|\vec v|^2$ and no resolution is needed.
solution: $\vec v_1\parallel\vec u$ and $\vec v_2\perp\vec u$, hence $\vec v_1\cdot\vec v_2=0$.
Then $|\vec v|^2=|\vec v_1+\vec v_2|^2=|\vec v_1|^2+|\vec v_2|^2+2\vec v_1\cdot\vec v_2=|\vec v_1|^2+|\vec v_2|^2$.
From the angle: $\cos^2\theta=\frac{(\vec u\cdot\vec v)^2}{|\vec u|^2|\vec v|^2}=\frac{25}{10\,|\vec v|^2}=\frac{5}{28}$.
Hence $|\vec v_1|^2+|\vec v_2|^2=14$ (the individual values $\frac52$ and $\frac{23}{2}$ are never needed).

useful_results: If $\vec v=\vec v_1+\vec v_2$ with $\vec v_1\perp\vec v_2$, then $|\vec v|^2=|\vec v_1|^2+|\vec v_2|^2$ (Pythagoras).

Component of $\vec v$ along $\vec u$: $\vec v_1=\frac{\vec u\cdot\vec v}{|\vec u|^2}\vec u$, with $|\vec v_1|=\frac{|\vec u\cdot\vec v|}{|\vec u|}=|\vec v|\,|\cos\theta|$; the perpendicular part has $|\vec v_2|=|\vec v|\sin\theta$.
Instance here: $\alpha=\frac{\vec u\cdot\vec v}{|\vec u|^2}=\frac{5}{10}=\frac12$ and $|\vec v_1|^2=|\vec v|^2\cos^2\theta=14\cdot\frac{5}{28}=\frac52$.
Check the sign of $\lambda>0$ before using it: $\lambda^2=9$ gives two values, only $\lambda=3$ is allowed.

concepts: Dot and cross product of unit vectors
questions.question: Let the angle $\theta,\ 0<\theta<\frac\pi2$ between two unit vectors $\hat a$ and $\hat b$ be $\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{65}}{9}\right)$. If the vector $\vec c=3\hat a+6\hat b+9(\hat a\times\hat b)$, then the value of $9(\vec c\cdot\hat a)-3(\vec c\cdot\hat b)$ is:
questions.key_idea: $\hat a\times\hat b$ is perpendicular to both $\hat a$ and $\hat b$, so it drops out of every dot product.
solution: $\vec c=3\hat a+6\hat b+9(\hat a\times\hat b)$ and $\sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt{65}}{9}$ with $0<\theta<\frac\pi2$.
$\vec c\cdot\hat a=3|\hat a|^2+6\,\hat a\cdot\hat b+9\,\hat a\cdot(\hat a\times\hat b)=3+6\cdot\frac49+0=3+\frac{24}{9}=\frac{51}{9}$.
$\vec c\cdot\hat b=3\,\hat a\cdot\hat b+6|\hat b|^2+9\,\hat b\cdot(\hat a\times\hat b)=3\cdot\frac49+6+0=\frac{12}{9}+6=\frac{22}{3}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Combine first: $9(\vec c\cdot\hat a)-3(\vec c\cdot\hat b)=\vec c\cdot(9\hat a-3\hat b)$, and the cross-product part vanishes at once.
solution: By linearity, $9(\vec c\cdot\hat a)-3(\vec c\cdot\hat b)=\vec c\cdot\left(9\hat a-3\hat b\right)$.
$\hat a\times\hat b$ is perpendicular to $9\hat a-3\hat b$ (a vector in the plane of $\hat a,\hat b$), so the $9(\hat a\times\hat b)$ term contributes $0$.
$\left(3\hat a+6\hat b\right)\cdot\left(9\hat a-3\hat b\right)=27-9\,\hat a\cdot\hat b+54\,\hat a\cdot\hat b-18=9+45\,\hat a\cdot\hat b$.

useful_results: $\vec a\times\vec b$ is perpendicular to every vector in the plane of $\vec a$ and $\vec b$: $(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot(p\vec a+q\vec b)=0$ for all scalars $p,q$.

For unit vectors at angle $\theta$: $\hat a\cdot\hat b=\cos\theta$, $|\hat a\times\hat b|=\sin\theta$; if $\sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt{n}}{m}$ with $n+k^2=m^2$, then $\cos\theta=\frac km$ (here $65+16=81$).
Inverse-sine given with $0<\theta<\frac\pi2$ fixes the sign of $\cos\theta$; without that range both signs of $\cos\theta$ would be possible.
The combination $9(\vec c\cdot\hat a)-3(\vec c\cdot\hat b)$ is a dot with the single vector $9\hat a-3\hat b$; always look for such a regrouping before computing separately.

concepts: Line perpendicular to two given lines
Symmetric (Cartesian) equation of a line
questions.question: If the equation of the line passing through the point $\left(0,-\frac12,0\right)$ and perpendicular to the lines $\vec r=\lambda\left(\hat i+a\hat j+b\hat k\right)$ and $\vec r=\left(\hat i-\hat j-6\hat k\right)+\mu\left(-b\hat i+a\hat j+5\hat k\right)$ is $\frac{x-1}{-2}=\frac{y+4}{d}=\frac{z-c}{-4}$, then $a+b+c+d$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The given point lies on the line, fixing $c,d$; then the direction is perpendicular to both given directions.
solution: The line has direction ratios $(-2,d,-4)=(-2,7,-4)$, and is perpendicular to the first line, direction $(1,a,b)$: $-2+7a-4b=0\ \ldots(1)$.
Perpendicular to the second line, direction $(-b,a,5)$: $2b+7a-20=0\ \ldots(2)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: A line perpendicular to two lines is parallel to the cross product of their directions, so match $(-2,7,-4)$ to that cross product.
solution: Cross product of the two directions: $(1,a,b)\times(-b,a,5)=\left(5a-ab,\ -b^2-5,\ a+ab\right)$.
The required line is parallel to this, so $(5a-ab,\ -b^2-5,\ a+ab)=k(-2,7,-4)$ for some $k\neq0$.
Adding the first and third components: $6a=-6k$, so $a=-k$.
Second component: $-b^2-5=-14=7k$, so $k=-2$ and $a=2$. The first component checks: $a(5-b)=4=-2k$.
The point $\left(0,-\frac12,0\right)$ on the line gives $d=7$, $c=2$ as before, so $a+b+c+d=2+3+2+7=14$.

useful_results: A line perpendicular to two lines with directions $\vec p,\vec q$ has direction $\vec p\times\vec q$ (or any multiple); equivalently the two dot conditions $\vec d\cdot\vec p=0$, $\vec d\cdot\vec q=0$.
Substituting a point known to lie on a symmetric line into $\frac{x-x_1}{l}=\frac{y-y_1}{m}=\frac{z-z_1}{n}$ gives equal ratios that fix unknown constants in the line.
Direction ratios are only fixed up to a scalar, so $(-2,d,-4)$ with $d=7$ is the direction $(-2,7,-4)$ exactly; the given $-2,-4$ pin the scale.
Perpendicular lines do not have to intersect; 'perpendicular' refers only to the directions.

concepts: Magnitude of sum and difference of vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ be vectors of the same magnitude such that $\frac{|\vec a+\vec b|+|\vec a-\vec b|}{|\vec a+\vec b|-|\vec a-\vec b|}=\sqrt2+1$. Then $\frac{|\vec a+\vec b|^2}{|\vec a|^2}$ is:
questions.key_idea: For equal magnitudes, $|\vec a+\vec b|=2|\vec a|\cos\frac\theta2$ and $|\vec a-\vec b|=2|\vec a|\sin\frac\theta2$, turning the ratio into $\tan\left(\frac\pi4+\frac\theta2\right)$.
solution: Let $|\vec a|=|\vec b|=P$ and let $\theta$ be the angle between them.
$\frac{|\vec a+\vec b|+|\vec a-\vec b|}{|\vec a+\vec b|-|\vec a-\vec b|}=\frac{\cos\frac\theta2+\sin\frac\theta2}{\cos\frac\theta2-\sin\frac\theta2}=\frac{1+\tan\frac\theta2}{1-\tan\frac\theta2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Componendo-dividendo gives $|\vec a+\vec b|:|\vec a-\vec b|$, and the parallelogram law $|\vec a+\vec b|^2+|\vec a-\vec b|^2=4|\vec a|^2$ finishes with no angle.
solution: Let $S=|\vec a+\vec b|$, $D=|\vec a-\vec b|$ and $r=\frac{S+D}{S-D}=\sqrt2+1$.
Parallelogram law with $|\vec a|=|\vec b|$: $S^2+D^2=2|\vec a|^2+2|\vec b|^2=4|\vec a|^2$.

useful_results: For $|\vec a|=|\vec b|=P$ at angle $\theta$: $|\vec a+\vec b|=2P\cos\frac\theta2$, $|\vec a-\vec b|=2P\sin\frac\theta2$, and $(\vec a+\vec b)\perp(\vec a-\vec b)$ (the diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular).
Parallelogram law: $|\vec a+\vec b|^2+|\vec a-\vec b|^2=2\left(|\vec a|^2+|\vec b|^2\right)$ for any two vectors.
$\frac{\cos x+\sin x}{\cos x-\sin x}=\tan\left(\frac\pi4+x\right)$; recognise it, and remember $\tan\frac{3\pi}{8}=\sqrt2+1$, $\tan\frac\pi8=\sqrt2-1$.
Componendo-dividendo: $\frac{p+q}{p-q}=r\Rightarrow\frac pq=\frac{r+1}{r-1}$ (valid for $p\ne q$).

concepts: Area of a triangle with base on a line
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: Let the vertices $Q$ and $R$ of the triangle $PQR$ lie on the line $\frac{x+3}{5}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z+4}{3}$, $QR=5$ and the coordinates of the point $P$ be $(0,2,3)$. If the area of the triangle $PQR$ is $\frac mn$, then:
questions.key_idea: Area is $\frac12\cdot QR\cdot PM$, where $PM$ is the perpendicular from $P$ to the line.
solution: $Q,R$ lie on the given line $L$ and $QR=5$; let $M$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P(0,2,3)$ to $L$.
A general point of $L$: $M(5\lambda-3,\ 2\lambda+1,\ 3\lambda-4)$. Direction ratios of $PM$: $(5\lambda-3,\ 2\lambda-1,\ 3\lambda-7)$.
questions.correction_note: The last line of the PDF's solution reads '$2m-5\sqrt{21}\,n=10$'. From $\frac12\cdot5\cdot\sqrt{21}=\frac mn$ the correct relation is $2m-5\sqrt{21}\,n=0$ (option 1, which is what the answer key marks). Only that last line was changed.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the distance formula $\frac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$ directly instead of finding the foot of the perpendicular.
solution: Take $A(-3,1,-4)$ on the line and direction $\vec d=(5,2,3)$ with $|\vec d|^2=38$. Then $\overrightarrow{AP}=(3,1,7)$.
Area $=\frac12\cdot QR\cdot PM=\frac52\sqrt{21}$, so $\frac mn=\frac{5\sqrt{21}}{2}$ and $2m-5\sqrt{21}\,n=0$.

useful_results: Distance from point $P$ to the line through $A$ with direction $\vec d$: $\frac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$; equivalently $\sqrt{|\overrightarrow{AP}|^2-\left(\frac{\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|}\right)^2}$.
If two vertices of a triangle slide along a line with fixed length $QR$, the area is constant, $\frac12\,QR\cdot d(P,\text{line})$; where on the line they sit is irrelevant.
Rational $\frac mn$ forces $\sqrt{21}$ to be cancelled by the other side: read the options as $\frac mn=\frac{5\sqrt{21}}{2}$, so $2m=5\sqrt{21}\,n$.

concepts: Tetrahedron with mutually perpendicular edges (areas of faces)
questions.question: Let $ABCD$ be a tetrahedron such that the edges $AB$, $AC$ and $AD$ are mutually perpendicular. Let the areas of the triangles $ABC$, $ACD$ and $ADB$ be $5$, $6$ and $7$ square units respectively. Then the area (in square units) of the $\triangle BCD$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: At a right-angled corner the square of the opposite face's area is the sum of the squares of the three other faces' areas (de Gua's theorem).
solution: Since $AB,AC,AD$ are mutually perpendicular, $A$ is a right-angled corner and $BCD$ is the face opposite to it.
By de Gua's theorem: $\text{Ar}(\triangle BCD)=\sqrt{\left(\text{Ar}(\triangle ABC)\right)^2+\left(\text{Ar}(\triangle ACD)\right)^2+\left(\text{Ar}(\triangle ADB)\right)^2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $A$ at the origin and $B,C,D$ on the axes; compute the area of $BCD$ with a cross product, which also proves the theorem.

useful_results: de Gua's theorem (3D Pythagoras): for a tetrahedron with a right-angled vertex, $S_{\text{hyp}}^2=S_1^2+S_2^2+S_3^2$ for the areas of the three right-angled faces and the opposite face.

Reason: each right-angled face is the projection of face $BCD$ onto a coordinate plane, with area $S\cos\alpha_i$ where $\cos^2\alpha_1+\cos^2\alpha_2+\cos^2\alpha_3=1$ for the direction cosines of the normal.
With the edges $p,q,r$ along the axes, the three corner-face areas are $\frac{pq}{2},\frac{qr}{2},\frac{rp}{2}$ and $\text{Ar}(BCD)=\frac12\sqrt{p^2q^2+q^2r^2+r^2p^2}$.
Check: for $p=q=r=1$ the faces are $\frac12$ each and $BCD$ is equilateral with side $\sqrt2$, area $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$; and $\sqrt{3\cdot\frac14}=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

concepts: Shortest distance between skew lines
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: Line $L_1$ passes through the point $(1,2,3)$ and is parallel to the $z$-axis. Line $L_2$ passes through the point $(\lambda,5,6)$ and is parallel to the $y$-axis. Let for $\lambda=\lambda_1,\lambda_2$, $\lambda_2<\lambda_1$, the shortest distance between the two lines be $3$. Then the square of the distance of the point $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,7)$ from the line $L_1$ is:
questions.key_idea: Both lines are parallel to axes, so the common perpendicular is along the third axis and the distance is simply $|\lambda-1|$.
solution: Direction vectors: $\vec p=(0,0,1)$ and $\vec q=(0,1,0)$, with $\vec p\times\vec q=(-1,0,0)$, $|\vec p\times\vec q|=1$.
Join of the points: $\overrightarrow{AB}=(\lambda-1,\ 3,\ 3)$. Shortest distance $=\frac{|\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot(\vec p\times\vec q)|}{|\vec p\times\vec q|}=|\lambda-1|=3$.
The point is $P(4,-2,7)$. Let the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $L_1$ be $Q(1,2,t+3)$ (a point of $L_1$).
$\overrightarrow{PQ}=(-3,4,t-4)$ must be perpendicular to $(0,0,1)$: $t-4=0$, so $t=4$ and $Q=(1,2,7)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Project onto the $xy$-plane: $L_1$ becomes the point $(1,2)$ and $L_2$ the line $x=\lambda$, so distances become plane distances.
solution: $L_1$ is parallel to the $z$-axis and $L_2$ to the $y$-axis. Viewed from above (projecting onto the $xy$-plane), $L_1$ is the single point $(1,2)$ and $L_2$ is the vertical line $x=\lambda$.
The shortest distance between the two lines equals the distance from the point $(1,2)$ to the line $x=\lambda$, which is $|\lambda-1|=3$, so $\lambda_1=4$, $\lambda_2=-2$.
The distance of the point $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,7)=(4,-2,7)$ from the vertical line $L_1$ is likewise its distance from $(1,2)$ in the $xy$-plane (the $z$-coordinate is irrelevant).
$\sqrt{(4-1)^2+(-2-2)^2}=\sqrt{25}=5$, so the square of the distance is $25$.

useful_results: A line parallel to the $z$-axis projects to a single point in the $xy$-plane; distances from it, and between it and another line, can then be read in that plane.
For lines parallel to two different coordinate axes, the shortest distance equals the difference of the coordinate along the third axis: here $|x_2-x_1|$.
Distance of $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ from the line through $(a,b,\cdot)$ parallel to the $z$-axis is $\sqrt{(x_0-a)^2+(y_0-b)^2}$.
A condition like $|\lambda-1|=3$ always gives two values; the question's ordering ($\lambda_2<\lambda_1$) decides which is which.

concepts: Line through a point meeting two given lines
Determinant (area/volume style) evaluation
questions.question: Let a line passing through the point $(4,1,0)$ intersect the line $L_1:\ \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z-3}{4}$ at the point $A(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ and the line $L_2:\ x-6=y=-z+4$ at the point $B(a,b,c)$. Then $\left|\begin{matrix}1&0&1\\ \alpha&\beta&\gamma\\ a&b&c\end{matrix}\right|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $P,A,B$ collinear gives proportional direction ratios of $PA$ and $PB$; two parameters $p,q$ then fix $A$ and $B$.
solution: Direction ratios of $PA$: $(2p-3,\ 3p+1,\ 4p+3)$. Direction ratios of $PB$: $(q+2,\ q-1,\ 4-q)$.
First two ratios equal: $(2p-3)(q-1)=(3p+1)(q+2)$, which simplifies to $pq+8p+4q-1=0\ \ldots(1)$ (the PDF prints this with typos).
Second and third ratios equal: $(3p+1)(4-q)=(4p+3)(q-1)$, which simplifies to $7pq-16p+4q-7=0\ \ldots(2)$.
Solving (1) and (2): $pq=-3$, $p=-1$, $q=3$. (The pair also satisfies the first and third ratios.)
questions.correction_note: The PDF's equation (1) is printed as 'pq + rp + 4q - 1 = 0' (rp should be 8p; also a stray 'z' in the intermediate line). Correct: pq + 8p + 4q - 1 = 0. Equations (1) and (2) alone also admit a spurious pair p=-1/3, q=1 (it fails the third ratio, as q-1=0 makes PB have zero y-component but PA does not), and the PDF jumps to 'pq = -3' without showing the step. Final values p=-1, q=3 and the answer 8 are right; checked by solving all three proportionality conditions symbolically.

alternate_solutions.idea: $B$ lies in the plane through $P$ and $L_1$ (collinearity forces coplanarity), so intersect that plane with $L_2$.
solution: Line $PAB$ meets $L_1$ at $A$, so $B$ lies in the plane $\Pi$ containing $P$ and $L_1$. Take $M=(1,2,3)\in L_1$, direction $\vec d=(2,3,4)$.

useful_results: To find a line through $P$ meeting two skew lines $L_1,L_2$: the plane through $P$ and $L_1$ meets $L_2$ at exactly one point $B$ (if not parallel); the line $PB$ is then the unique transversal.
Collinearity of three points via direction ratios gives a system of two independent equations; always check the third ratio, since a pair of cross-multiplied equations can admit spurious solutions.
$\left|\begin{matrix}1&0&1\\ \alpha&\beta&\gamma\\ a&b&c\end{matrix}\right|=(\beta c-\gamma b)+(\alpha b-\beta a)$: expand along the first row, which has a zero.
Parametrise each line with its own parameter ($p$ for $L_1$, $q$ for $L_2$) so the two points stay independent.

concepts: Direction cosines of a line
questions.question: Each of the angles $\beta$ and $\gamma$ that a given line makes with the positive $y$- and $z$-axes, respectively, is half of the angle that this line makes with the positive $x$-axis. Then the sum of all possible values of the angle $\beta$ is:
questions.key_idea: Use $\cos^2\alpha+\cos^2\beta+\cos^2\gamma=1$ with $\beta=\gamma=\frac\alpha2$, then $\cos^2\frac\alpha2=\frac{1+\cos\alpha}{2}$.
solution: Let the angle with the $x$-axis be $\alpha$. Then $\beta=\frac\alpha2$ and $\gamma=\frac\alpha2$.
Hence $\alpha=\frac\pi2$ or $\alpha=\pi$ (angles with an axis lie in $[0,\pi]$).
Sum of all possible values of $\beta$: $\frac\pi4+\frac\pi2=\frac{3\pi}{4}$, option (1).
useful_results: Direction cosines $l=\cos\alpha,\ m=\cos\beta,\ n=\cos\gamma$ satisfy $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$; equivalently $\sin^2\alpha+\sin^2\beta+\sin^2\gamma=2$.
Angles a line makes with the axes lie in $[0,\pi]$ (direction reversed gives supplementary angles); an angle of $0$ or $\pi$ means the line is along that axis.
Half-angle form: $2\cos^2\frac\alpha2=1+\cos\alpha$ reduces the equation to a quadratic in $\cos\alpha$ (here $\cos\alpha(\cos\alpha+1)=0$).
Check both solutions: $\alpha=\frac\pi2$ gives $(0,\frac1{\sqrt2},\frac1{\sqrt2})$ and $\alpha=\pi$ gives $(-1,0,0)$; both have unit length.

concepts: Foot of perpendicular from a point to a line
Dot product of position vectors
questions.question: Let $A$ and $B$ be two distinct points on the line $L:\ \frac{x-6}{3}=\frac{y-7}{2}=\frac{z-7}{-2}$. Both $A$ and $B$ are at a distance $2\sqrt{17}$ from the foot of the perpendicular drawn from the point $(1,2,3)$ on the line $L$. If $O$ is the origin, then $\overrightarrow{OA}\cdot\overrightarrow{OB}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Find the foot $M$ first; then $A$ and $B$ are the two points of $L$ at distance $2\sqrt{17}$ on either side of $M$.
solution: Write $\frac{x-6}{3}=\frac{y-7}{2}=\frac{z-7}{-2}=\lambda$. A point of $L$ is $M(3\lambda+6,\ 2\lambda+7,\ -2\lambda+7)$; the direction vector of $L$ is $\vec b=3\hat i+2\hat j-2\hat k$.
Let $M$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P(1,2,3)$: $\overrightarrow{PM}=(3\lambda+5,\ 2\lambda+5,\ -2\lambda+4)$ and $\overrightarrow{PM}\cdot\vec b=0$.

The points at distance $2\sqrt{17}$ from $M$ have parameter $\mu$ with $\left(3\mu+3\right)^2+\left(2\mu+2\right)^2+\left(-2\mu-2\right)^2=17\cdot4$ (a point $(3\mu+6,\,2\mu+7,\,-2\mu+7)$ minus $M$ is $(\mu+1)(3,2,-2)$).
$\mu=1$ gives $(9,9,5)$ and $\mu=-3$ gives $(-3,1,13)$. These are $A$ and $B$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $A,B=M\pm\vec v$ are symmetric about $M$, so $\overrightarrow{OA}\cdot\overrightarrow{OB}=|OM|^2-|\vec v|^2$ with no coordinates for $A,B$.
solution: The foot is $M(3,5,9)$ (from $\overrightarrow{PM}\perp\vec b$, as before), so $\overrightarrow{OM}=(3,5,9)$ and $|OM|^2=9+25+81=115$.

$A$ and $B$ lie on $L$ at distance $2\sqrt{17}$ on either side of $M$, so $\overrightarrow{OA}=\overrightarrow{OM}+\vec v$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\overrightarrow{OM}-\vec v$ with $|\vec v|=2\sqrt{17}$.

useful_results: Two points symmetric about $M$: $(\vec m+\vec v)\cdot(\vec m-\vec v)=|\vec m|^2-|\vec v|^2$ (difference of squares); it is the power of the point $O$ with respect to the sphere on $AB$ as diameter.
Foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to a line: put the general point $M$ of the line, impose $\overrightarrow{PM}\cdot\vec d=0$; the answer is linear in the parameter.
Points at a given distance $k$ from $M$ on the line: $M\pm\frac{k}{|\vec d|}\vec d$; here $\frac{2\sqrt{17}}{\sqrt{17}}=2$, so $M\pm2(3,2,-2)$.
Two points 'on both sides' of the foot always come in a symmetric pair, so the pair $A,B$ is unordered and the product is the same.

concepts: Angle between two lines
Area of a triangle (isosceles with given sides)
questions.question: Let $A$ be the point of intersection of the lines $L_1:\ \frac{x-7}{1}=\frac{y-5}{0}=\frac{z-3}{-1}$ and $L_2:\ \frac{x-1}{3}=\frac{y+3}{4}=\frac{z+7}{5}$. Let $B$ and $C$ be the points on the lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ respectively such that $AB=AC=\sqrt{15}$. Then the square of the area of the triangle $ABC$ is:
questions.key_idea: Only the angle at $A$ matters: area $=\frac12\,AB\cdot AC\sin\theta$ with $\theta$ the angle between the lines.
solution: The lines meet at $A=(7,5,3)$ (parameters $s=0$ on $L_1$ and $t=2$ on $L_2$); $B$ and $C$ lie on $L_1$ and $L_2$ at distance $\sqrt{15}$ from $A$.
Direction vectors: $\vec d_1=(1,0,-1)$, $|\vec d_1|=\sqrt2$; $\vec d_2=(3,4,5)$, $|\vec d_2|=\sqrt{50}$; $\vec d_1\cdot\vec d_2=3-5=-2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use Lagrange's identity: area$^2=\frac14\left(|AB|^2|AC|^2-(\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC})^2\right)$, so no square roots of $\sin\theta$ appear.
solution: Hence $(\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC})^2=9$ for every choice of the signs.

useful_results: Area of a triangle with two sides $p,q$ at angle $\theta$: $\frac12pq\sin\theta$, and $\text{Area}^2=\frac14\left(p^2q^2-(\vec p\cdot\vec q)^2\right)$ (Lagrange identity $|\vec p\times\vec q|^2=p^2q^2-(\vec p\cdot\vec q)^2$).
The choice of which side of $A$ the points $B,C$ lie on changes the angle at $A$ from $\theta$ to $\pi-\theta$ but not $\sin\theta$, so the area is the same.
Angle between lines uses $|\cos\theta|=\frac{|\vec d_1\cdot\vec d_2|}{|\vec d_1||\vec d_2|}$ (acute angle); for triangle areas the sign is irrelevant.
Intersection of $L_1$ and $L_2$: equate coordinates, solve two of them for the parameters, verify with the third (here $s=0$, $t=2$).

concepts: Foot of perpendicular on a line
Area of a triangle in 3D
questions.question: Consider the lines $L_1:\ x-1=y-2=z$ and $L_2:\ x-2=y=z-1$. Let the feet of the perpendiculars from the point $P(5,1,-3)$ on the lines $L_1$ and $L_2$ be $Q$ and $R$ respectively. If the area of the triangle $PQR$ is $A$, then $4A^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Both lines have direction $(1,1,1)$, so each foot comes from $\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot(1,1,1)=0$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $\triangle PQR$ is isosceles ($PQ=PR$): find the three side lengths and use the height to the base instead of a cross product.
solution: Feet as in the main solution: $Q=(1,2,0)$ and $R=(2,0,1)$ (each from $\overrightarrow{P\,\cdot}\perp(1,1,1)$).
$PQ^2=16+1+9=26$ and $PR^2=9+1+16=26$, so $PQ=PR$ and the triangle is isosceles with base $QR$.

useful_results: Foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the line through $A$ with direction $\vec d$: $Q=A+\frac{(\vec P-\vec A)\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}\vec d$; for the lines here $\vec d=(1,1,1)$ and the condition is the coordinate sum of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ equal to $0$.
If a triangle has two equal sides, the height to the third side is $\sqrt{p^2-(c/2)^2}$; no cross product is needed.

$4A^2=|\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{PR}|^2=|PQ|^2|PR|^2-(\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\overrightarrow{PR})^2$. Here $\overrightarrow{PQ}\cdot\overrightarrow{PR}=12-1+12=23$, so $26\cdot26-23^2=676-529=147$.
Two parallel lines have a common perpendicular plane: the feet of perpendiculars from $P$ lie in the plane through $P$ perpendicular to the lines, here $x+y+z=3$.

concepts: Perpendicular vectors and dot product of unit vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ be two unit vectors such that the angle between them is $\frac\pi3$. If $\lambda\vec a+2\vec b$ and $3\vec a-\lambda\vec b$ are perpendicular to each other, then the number of values of $\lambda$ in $[-1,3]$ is:
questions.key_idea: Perpendicularity gives a quadratic in $\lambda$, and the roots must then be compared with the interval $[-1,3]$.
solution: Expanding: $3\lambda|\vec a|^2-\lambda^2\,\vec a\cdot\vec b+6\,\vec a\cdot\vec b-2\lambda|\vec b|^2=0$.
So the number of values of $\lambda$ in $[-1,3]$ is $0$, option (4).
questions.correction_note: The PDF expands the dot product wrongly: it writes '3λ - λ² + 6a.b - λ a.b = 0' and gets '2λ² - 5λ + 6 = 0' (D = 25 - 48 < 0, no real root). The correct expansion is 3λ - λ²(a.b) + 6(a.b) - 2λ = 0, i.e. λ² - 2λ - 6 = 0, which has real roots 1 ± √7, both outside [-1, 3]. The final answer 0 (option 4) is still correct, but for a different reason (roots exist but lie outside the interval).

alternate_solutions.idea: Do not solve the quadratic: $f(\lambda)=-\frac{\lambda^2}{2}+\lambda+3$ is concave, so checking its endpoint values on $[-1,3]$ and its maximum shows it never vanishes there.
solution: Place $\vec a=(1,0)$ and $\vec b=\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$ in a plane (unit vectors at $60^\circ$).
$f$ is a downward parabola with vertex at $\lambda=1$, where $f(1)=\frac72>0$; on $[-1,3]$ the minimum is at an endpoint: $f(-1)=\frac32>0$ and $f(3)=\frac32>0$.
So $f(\lambda)>0$ throughout $[-1,3]$: the vectors are never perpendicular there, so the number of values is $0$.

useful_results: Expand dot products with care: $(p\vec a+q\vec b)\cdot(r\vec a+s\vec b)=pr|\vec a|^2+(ps+qr)\,\vec a\cdot\vec b+qs|\vec b|^2$. Sign slips here are the most common source of wrong quadratics.
A quadratic's roots can be outside an interval even when real; compare them (or evaluate $f$ at endpoints and the vertex) before counting.
For a concave quadratic on an interval, $f>0$ at both endpoints implies $f>0$ throughout; for a convex one the vertex must be checked.
Using coordinates for two unit vectors at angle $\theta$: $\vec a=(1,0)$, $\vec b=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ keeps every dot product mechanical.

concepts: Line through a point with given direction
Area of a triangle in 3D
questions.question: Let a line pass through two distinct points $P(-2,-1,3)$ and $Q$, and be parallel to the vector $3\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k$. If the distance of the point $Q$ from the point $R(1,3,3)$ is $5$, then the square of the area of $\triangle PQR$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $Q=P+\lambda(3,2,2)$; the condition $QR=5$ gives a quadratic whose root $\lambda=0$ is rejected because $Q\ne P$.
solution: $\lambda=0$ or $\lambda=2$. $\lambda=0$ gives $Q=P$, which is not allowed (distinct points), so $\lambda=2$ and $Q=(4,3,7)$.
$\overrightarrow{PQ}=6\hat i+4\hat j+4\hat k$ and $\overrightarrow{QR}=-3\hat i+0\hat j-4\hat k$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Notice $PR=QR=5$: the triangle is isosceles, so $PQ=2\times$(foot of $R$ on the line to $P$) and the area follows from base and height.
solution: Hence the foot $F$ of the perpendicular from $R$ to the line $PQ$ is the midpoint of $PQ$.
Height: $RF^2=\frac{|\overrightarrow{PR}\times\vec d|^2}{|\vec d|^2}$ with $\vec d=(3,2,2)$: $(3,4,0)\times(3,2,2)=(8,-6,-6)$, so $RF^2=\frac{136}{17}=8$.

useful_results: A point on a line with direction $\vec d$ through $P$ at distance $k$ from a given point $R$ gives a quadratic in $\lambda$ with $\lambda=0$ as a root exactly when $PR=k$; then the other root is the reflection of $P$ across the foot of $R$.

If $RP=RQ$ then the foot of the perpendicular from $R$ to $PQ$ is the midpoint; so $\overrightarrow{PQ}=2\,\text{proj}_{\vec d}\overrightarrow{PR}$ and $Q=P+\frac{2\,\overrightarrow{PR}\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}\vec d$ (here $\frac{2\cdot17}{17}=2$).
$\Delta^2=\frac14|\overrightarrow{PQ}\times\overrightarrow{QR}|^2$ avoids a square root until the end.
The condition 'distinct points' is exactly what discards the trivial root $\lambda=0$; always read it as a constraint.

concepts: Tetrahedron: altitude, volume and median line
Position vector of a point on a line
questions.question: Let the position vectors of the vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ of a tetrahedron $ABCD$ be $\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k$, $\hat i+3\hat j-2\hat k$ and $2\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$ respectively. The altitude from the vertex $D$ to the opposite face $ABC$ meets the median line segment through $A$ of the triangle $ABC$ at the point $E$. If the length of $AD$ is $\frac{\sqrt{110}}{3}$ and the volume of the tetrahedron is $\frac{\sqrt{805}}{6\sqrt2}$, then the position vector of $E$ is:
questions.key_idea: $E$ is the foot of the altitude, so $AE^2=AD^2-h^2$ with $h$ from the volume; $E$ then sits on the median at that distance from $A$.
solution: $A=(1,2,1)$, $B=(1,3,-2)$, $C=(2,1,-1)$. $\overrightarrow{AB}=\hat j-3\hat k$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=\hat i-\hat j-2\hat k$.
$DE\perp$ plane $ABC$ and $E$ is in that plane, so $AE^2=AD^2-DE^2=\frac{110}{9}-\frac{23}{2}=\frac{220-207}{18}=\frac{13}{18}$.
Midpoint of $BC$ is $\left(\frac32,2,-\frac32\right)$, so the median from $A$ has direction ratios $\left(\frac12,0,-\frac52\right)\propto(1,0,-5)$.
$E$ lies on the median segment from $A$ to the midpoint of $BC$, i.e. $0\le\lambda\le\frac12$, so $\lambda=+\frac16$ (the other root lies on the far side of $A$, outside the triangle).
questions.correction_note: The PDF obtains lambda = +-1/6 and then writes E(7/6, 2, 1/6) without saying why the + sign is taken. The sign must be chosen because E lies on the median SEGMENT (0 <= lambda <= 1/2); lambda = -1/6 gives (5/6, 2, 11/6), a point on the extension beyond A. One step (the choice of sign) was added; all numbers in the PDF were verified correct.

alternate_solutions.idea: $E$ must lie in the plane $ABC$ and on the median segment; test the options against just these two facts.
solution: Plane $ABC$ has normal $(5,3,1)$ (from $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}$), so its equation is $5x+3y+z=5(1)+3(2)+1=12$.
Option (1) $\left(2,2,\frac16\right)$: $10+6+\frac16\neq12$, not in the plane. Option (4) $\left(\frac7{12},\frac13,\frac14\right)$: $\frac{35}{12}+1+\frac14=\frac{25}{6}\neq12$, not in the plane.
Option (2) $\left(\frac12,2,\frac72\right)$: $\frac52+6+\frac72=12$, in the plane, and it equals $A+\lambda(1,0,-5)$ with $\lambda=-\frac12$.
Option (3) $\left(\frac76,2,\frac16\right)$: $\frac{35}{6}+6+\frac16=12$, in the plane, and it equals $A+\lambda(1,0,-5)$ with $\lambda=+\frac16$.
The median segment from $A$ to the midpoint of $BC$ is $0\le\lambda\le\frac12$, so option (2) (with $\lambda=-\frac12$) lies off the segment and only option (3) is possible.
Consistency check with the data: $AE^2=26\cdot\frac1{36}=\frac{13}{18}=AD^2-h^2$, as obtained from the volume. Answer: option (3).
(This option-based route needs neither the volume nor $AD$; those values only confirm the choice.)

useful_results: The foot of the altitude from $D$ is the orthogonal projection of $D$ onto plane $ABC$, so $AD^2=AE^2+DE^2$ (Pythagoras in the right triangle $AED$) and $DE=h=\frac{3V}{\text{Ar}(ABC)}$.
Volume of a tetrahedron: $V=\frac13\times\text{base area}\times\text{height}=\frac16\left|[\overrightarrow{AB}\ \overrightarrow{AC}\ \overrightarrow{AD}]\right|$.

Median from $A$ goes toward the midpoint $\frac{\vec b+\vec c}{2}$; a point on the median segment has parameter between $0$ and the midpoint's parameter, which decides a $\pm$ sign from a squared-length equation.
Normal of the plane through three points is $\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}$; test a point $X$ for membership with $(\overrightarrow{AX})\cdot\vec n=0$.

concepts: Linear combination of vectors on a circle (arcs and central angles)
questions.question: Let the arc $AC$ of a circle subtend a right angle at the centre $O$. If the point $B$ on the arc $AC$ divides the arc $AC$ such that $\frac{\text{length of arc }AB}{\text{length of arc }BC}=\frac15$, and $\overrightarrow{OC}=\alpha\overrightarrow{OA}+\beta\overrightarrow{OB}$, then $\alpha+\sqrt2\left(\sqrt3-1\right)\beta$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Arc ratio $1:5$ of a $90^\circ$ arc gives $\angle AOB=15^\circ$, $\angle BOC=75^\circ$; then dot $\overrightarrow{OC}=\alpha\overrightarrow{OA}+\beta\overrightarrow{OB}$ with $\overrightarrow{OC}$ and $\overrightarrow{OA}$.
solution: Arcs $AB:BC=1:5$ with total $\frac\pi2$: arc $AB=x$, arc $BC=5x$ and $6x=\frac\pi2$, so $x=\frac\pi{12}$. Hence $\angle AOB=\frac\pi{12}$ and $\angle BOC=\frac{5\pi}{12}$ (the PDF's figure labels the two arcs the other way round, but its calculation uses these angles).
questions.correction_note: Two slips in the PDF: (i) its figure labels arc AB = 5x and arc BC = x, the reverse of the stated ratio AB/BC = 1/5, while its calculation actually uses angle AOB = pi/12 (cos(pi/12) in eq. (1)), which matches the question; (ii) in the line 'dot with OC' it writes alpha r^2 cos(pi/12) for OC.OA, which should be alpha r^2 cos(pi/2) = 0 (it is dropped in the next line). Corrected the labelling and that term. Final answer 2 - sqrt(3) verified numerically.

alternate_solutions.idea: Coordinates: put $A=(1,0)$, $C=(0,1)$, $B=(\cos15^\circ,\sin15^\circ)$ and read $\alpha,\beta$ off the two components.
solution: Take $r=1$, $\overrightarrow{OA}=(1,0)$, $\overrightarrow{OC}=(0,1)$ (right angle at $O$) and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\left(\cos\frac\pi{12},\sin\frac\pi{12}\right)$ since arc $AB=\frac\pi{12}$.

useful_results: Arc length $=r\theta$, so equal radii turn an arc ratio into a ratio of central angles.

To split a vector as $\alpha\vec u+\beta\vec v$ in a plane, dot with a vector perpendicular to one of them: dot with $\overrightarrow{OA}$ (perpendicular to $\overrightarrow{OC}$) gives $\alpha$ in terms of $\beta$ at once.
Standard values: $\cos15^\circ=\frac{\sqrt6+\sqrt2}{4}=\frac{\sqrt3+1}{2\sqrt2}$, $\sin15^\circ=\frac{\sqrt6-\sqrt2}{4}=\frac{\sqrt3-1}{2\sqrt2}$, $\cot15^\circ=2+\sqrt3$, $\tan15^\circ=2-\sqrt3$.
Instance: the coefficient of $\overrightarrow{OA}$ is $-\cot15^\circ$ and of $\overrightarrow{OB}$ is $\operatorname{cosec}15^\circ$, by the law of sines in the vector triangle.

concepts: Section formula (internal division)
Scalar and vector products of position vectors
questions.question: Let the point $A$ divide the line segment joining the points $P(-1,-1,2)$ and $Q(5,5,10)$ internally in the ratio $r:1\ (r>0)$. If $O$ is the origin and $\left(\overrightarrow{OQ}\cdot\overrightarrow{OA}\right)-\frac15\left|\overrightarrow{OP}\times\overrightarrow{OA}\right|^2=10$, then the value of $r$ is:
questions.key_idea: $\overrightarrow{OP}\times\overrightarrow{OA}=\frac{r}{r+1}\,\overrightarrow{OP}\times\overrightarrow{OQ}$, so both terms become functions of $r$ alone.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $A=P+t(Q-P)$ with $t=\frac{r}{r+1}$; then $\overrightarrow{OP}\times\overrightarrow{OA}=t\,\overrightarrow{OP}\times\overrightarrow{OQ}$ and the equation is a quadratic in $t$.
solution: $A$ divides $PQ$ in the ratio $r:1$, so $\overrightarrow{OA}=(1-t)\overrightarrow{OP}+t\overrightarrow{OQ}$ with $t=\frac{r}{r+1}\in(0,1)$.

useful_results: If $A$ divides $PQ$ in the ratio $r:1$, then $\vec a=\frac{r\vec q+\vec p}{r+1}=(1-t)\vec p+t\vec q$ with $t=\frac{r}{r+1}$; products of $\vec a$ with $\vec p$ or $\vec q$ are linear or quadratic in $t$.
$\vec p\times\vec a=t\,(\vec p\times\vec q)$ and $\vec q\times\vec a=(1-t)\,(\vec q\times\vec p)$: crossing with an endpoint turns the cross product into a multiple of $\vec p\times\vec q$.
Lagrange's identity check: $|\vec p\times\vec q|^2=|\vec p|^2|\vec q|^2-(\vec p\cdot\vec q)^2=6\cdot150-100=800$.
Recover $r$ from $t$: $r=\frac{t}{1-t}$; $t=\frac78\Rightarrow r=7$.
